lessons.title: Work Plans and Time Management
lessons.description: Creating and using work plans, Gantt charts, milestones and contingencies for media production.
lessons.content_html:
Why Work Plans Matter in Media Production

Every media product — whether it is a film, website, or advertising campaign — goes through three phases of production: pre-production, production, and post-production. A work plan is the document that organises all of these phases into a clear, manageable schedule.

Without a work plan, teams risk missing deadlines, running over budget, and forgetting important tasks. In the media industry, where projects often involve large teams with different specialisms, a work plan ensures everyone knows what they should be doing and when.

Key Fact

A work plan is used to manage time, tasks, activities and resources for both individuals and large teams. It keeps every member of the production team on track.

Components of a Work Plan

The R093 exam expects you to know every component that makes up a work plan and explain the role each one plays. Here are the key components:

Phases — every media project is divided into pre-production, production and post-production. The work plan shows which tasks fall into which phase so nothing is attempted out of order.

Tasks and activities — the specific jobs that need completing. In pre-production this might include creating storyboards, writing scripts and booking locations. In production it could be filming, recording voiceovers and capturing photographs.

Workflow — the order in which tasks must be completed. Some tasks are dependent on others — for example, you cannot begin editing (post-production) until filming (production) is finished.

Timescales set start and end dates for each task, giving the team clear deadlines. Without timescales, work drifts and the final deadline is missed.

Milestones are significant checkpoints within the project — for example, “all filming completed” or “first edit reviewed by client.” They allow the project manager to check whether the project is on track at key moments.

A contingency is a backup plan for when things go wrong. If an actor is ill, a contingency might be to film scenes that do not require that actor. If a location becomes unavailable, a backup location should already be identified.

Resources

A work plan also lists the resources needed for the project. The specification groups these into three categories:

  • Hardware — cameras, microphones, lighting rigs, computers, SD cards, tripods
  • Software — editing suites (e.g. Adobe Premiere Pro), graphic design tools (e.g. Photoshop), audio editing software (e.g. Audacity)
  • People — camera operators, directors, sound technicians, editors, actors, graphic designers

Listing resources in advance ensures that budgets are accurate, equipment is booked, and the right people are available at the right time.

Gantt Charts

A Gantt chart is the most common way to present a work plan visually. Time runs along the horizontal axis (usually in days or weeks), and tasks are listed vertically. Each task is shown as a horizontal bar — the length of the bar shows how long the task will take.

Key Fact

Gantt charts are useful because they show task duration, overlapping tasks, dependencies and milestones at a glance. They help teams identify where tasks can run at the same time (parallel working) and where one task must finish before another can start.

Advantages:

  • Everyone knows their responsibilities and deadlines
  • Progress can be tracked and problems spotted early
  • Resources are allocated efficiently, reducing waste and cost
  • Contingencies mean unexpected problems do not derail the project
  • Milestones allow quality checks at key stages

Limitations:

  • Work plans take time to create and need updating as the project progresses
  • They cannot predict every possible problem
  • In very small teams or solo projects, a detailed work plan may feel excessive

Work Plans for Individuals vs Large Teams

An individual freelancer might use a simple to-do list or basic Gantt chart to track their own progress. A large production team — for example, a film crew — needs a much more detailed work plan showing which department handles each task, who is responsible, and how tasks interlink.

In a large team, the work plan also helps with communication. If the camera crew knows that the set will not be ready until Thursday, they can schedule other work for Monday to Wednesday. Without the work plan, they might arrive on set only to find it is not finished.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the R093 exam, you may be given a scenario and asked to explain why a work plan would benefit the production. Always link your answer to specific components — do not just say “it helps with planning.” Instead, explain how milestones, contingencies and timescales keep the project on track. Use the scenario details to give specific examples.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A work plan organises a media project into phases (pre-production, production, post-production) and lists all tasks, timescales, milestones, contingencies and resources.
  • Gantt charts are the standard visual format for work plans, showing task duration and overlap at a glance.
  • Work plans benefit both individuals and large teams by improving communication, tracking progress and ensuring resources are available when needed.

Award up to 4 marks:

practice_questions.text: A media company is planning a TV advertisement. Explain how a Gantt chart would help the company manage the production.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the differences between using a work plan for an individual freelancer compared to a large production team. In your answer, consider the advantages and any limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): A thorough discussion that clearly contrasts individual and team use, with specific examples of components (e.g. milestones, resources, contingencies). Considers both advantages and limitations for each. Well-structured response with reasoned conclusions.
Mid band (4-6): A reasonable discussion with some contrast between individual and team use. Some relevant examples but may lack detail or balance.
Lower band (1-3): A basic response that identifies some differences but with limited explanation. May describe work plans without clearly comparing the two contexts.

lessons.title: Mind Maps and Mood Boards
lessons.description: Using mind maps and mood boards to generate and present creative ideas for media products.
lessons.content_html:
Documents for Ideas Generation

Before any media product is created, the production team needs to generate and explore ideas. Two key documents are used at this stage: mind maps and mood boards. Both are classed as pre-production documents — they are created before the actual product is made.

The R093 exam requires you to know the purpose of each document, its components and conventions, the hardware and software used to create it, its users, when it is appropriate to use, what makes it effective, and how it could be improved.

Mind Maps

A mind map is a brainstorming tool. It starts with a central idea in the middle of the page and branches outward into related sub-topics. Each branch can split further, creating a web of connected ideas.

Key Fact

The purpose of a mind map is to generate and organise ideas. It helps the creator explore possibilities quickly, see connections between ideas, and ensure no aspect of the brief is overlooked.

A well-constructed mind map follows these conventions:

  • Central topic — the main subject or project brief is placed in the centre
  • Main branches — key categories or themes radiate outward from the centre
  • Sub-branches — more detailed ideas connect to the main branches
  • Keywords — short words or phrases are used, not full sentences
  • Colour coding — different colours for different branches help distinguish categories
  • Images and icons — small visuals can make branches more memorable

Mind maps can be created in two ways:

  • Hand drawn — using paper and coloured pens. Quick and flexible, but harder to edit and share.
  • Digital — using software such as MindMeister, XMind, or Coggle. Easy to edit, reorganise, and share with the team, but requires access to a computer and software.

Mood Boards

A mood board is a visual collection of images, colours, fonts, textures, and samples that represent the intended aesthetic of a media product. It communicates the overall “feel” of the project to the client and the production team.

Key Fact

The purpose of a mood board is to present the visual concept and communicate the intended style of a media product to clients, designers and other stakeholders before production begins.

An effective mood board typically includes:

  • Images — photographs, illustrations, or screenshots that reflect the intended visual style
  • Colour palette — a selection of colours that will be used across the product
  • Typography samples — examples of fonts and text styles
  • Textures and patterns — materials or surface effects that contribute to the feel
  • Annotations — brief notes explaining why each element has been included

Like mind maps, mood boards can be created in two forms:

  • Physical — printed images, fabric swatches, and colour chips arranged on a board. Useful when textures and materials need to be seen in real life, but difficult to share remotely.
  • Digital — created using software such as Canva, Adobe Spark, or Pinterest boards. Easy to update, share and present to remote clients, but physical textures cannot be conveyed accurately.

When to Use Each Document

Mind maps are best used at the very start of a project to brainstorm ideas before any visual direction has been decided. They are ideal for exploring content, themes and possible approaches.

Mood boards come after initial ideas have been generated. Once the team has a direction, the mood board communicates the visual style to clients and other team members. A graphic designer, web developer, or set designer would all use a mood board to ensure their work matches the agreed aesthetic.

An effective mind map is well-organised with clear branches, uses colour coding consistently, and covers all aspects of the brief. It can be improved by adding more detail to sub-branches, including small images, or reorganising branches so the most important ideas are more prominent.

An effective mood board has a clear visual theme, includes a range of relevant elements (images, colours, fonts), and is annotated so the viewer understands the choices. It can be improved by replacing low-quality images, adding annotations, or refining the colour palette to be more cohesive.

Users of These Documents

Mind maps are primarily used by the creative team and project manager during brainstorming sessions. Mood boards are used by a wider group including clients, designers, directors, and marketing teams to agree on the visual direction of the product.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In Section B of R093, you may be asked to recommend a pre-production document for a given scenario. If the scenario is about generating initial ideas, recommend a mind map and explain its purpose. If the scenario is about presenting a visual concept to a client, recommend a mood board. Always explain why the document is appropriate for that specific situation, not just what it is.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mind maps brainstorm and organise ideas using a central topic with branching sub-topics. They can be hand drawn or digital.
  • Mood boards communicate the visual style of a media product using images, colours, fonts and textures. They can be physical or digital.
  • Both documents are created in pre-production. Mind maps come first (ideas generation), mood boards follow (visual concept presentation).

Lower band (1-3): A basic response that identifies one or two improvements with limited explanation. May not compare physical and digital formats.

lessons.title: Asset Logs and Flowcharts
lessons.description: Organising assets with asset logs and planning user navigation using flowcharts.
lessons.content_html:
Documents for Designing and Planning Media Products

Once initial ideas have been generated (using mind maps and mood boards), the production team needs more detailed documents to plan the actual media product. The R093 specification covers six planning documents: asset logs, flowcharts, scripts, storyboards, visualisation diagrams and wireframe layouts. This lesson focuses on the first two: asset logs and flowcharts.

Asset Logs

An asset log is a table or spreadsheet that records every asset used in a media product. An asset is any resource that forms part of the final product — this includes images, audio files, video clips, graphics, fonts and text content.

Key Fact

The purpose of an asset log is to record and organise all assets used in a media product, ensuring the production team knows where every file came from, what format it is in, and whether copyright permission has been obtained.

A well-structured asset log typically includes columns for:

  • Asset name — a clear, descriptive file name (e.g. “hero-banner.jpg”)
  • Asset type — image, audio, video, graphic, font
  • File format — JPEG, PNG, MP3, WAV, MP4, etc.
  • Source — where the asset came from (original creation, stock library, client-provided)
  • Copyright/licence status — whether permission has been granted, what licence applies (e.g. Creative Commons), and any fees paid
  • Date acquired — when the asset was sourced or created
  • Used in — which part of the product the asset appears in

Asset logs can be created using spreadsheet software such as Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets. They are used by producers, editors, designers and project managers to keep track of resources and ensure all copyright obligations are met.

An asset log is appropriate whenever a media product uses multiple assets from different sources. This is especially important for commercial products where using an image or music track without permission could lead to legal action.

Flowcharts

A flowchart shows the structure and navigation of an interactive media product. It uses standard shapes connected by arrows to represent the sequence of steps, decisions and paths a user can take.

Key Fact

The purpose of a flowchart is to plan the navigation and structure of an interactive media product such as a website, app or game. It shows every page or screen, the decisions users make, and the paths they can follow.

Flowcharts use internationally recognised symbols:

  • Oval / rounded rectangle — start and end points (terminal)
  • Rectangle — a process or action (e.g. “Display homepage”)
  • Diamond — a decision point with Yes/No or multiple outcomes (e.g. “Is the user logged in?”)
  • Parallelogram — input or output of data
  • Arrows — show the direction of flow between steps

Flowcharts can be hand drawn or created using software such as Microsoft Visio, Lucidchart, or draw.io. Digital flowcharts are easier to edit and share.

When to Use Flowcharts

Flowcharts are most appropriate when planning interactive products where the user makes choices. Examples include:

  • A website with multiple pages and navigation menus
  • A mobile app with different screens and user journeys
  • A computer game with branching storylines or menu systems
  • An interactive quiz or e-learning module

Flowcharts are used by web developers, game designers, UX designers and project managers to agree on the product structure before building begins.

An effective asset log is complete (every asset is recorded), accurate (correct file formats and sources), and up to date. It can be improved by adding more detailed copyright information, standardising file naming conventions, or including thumbnail previews of visual assets.

An effective flowchart uses standard symbols consistently, has clear labels on every shape, and includes arrows showing all possible paths. It can be improved by adding colour coding for different sections, ensuring decision diamonds clearly show all outcomes, and testing the flowchart against user stories to check nothing is missing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When the exam asks you to recommend a pre-production document, think about what the scenario needs. If assets need organising and copyright tracking, recommend an asset log. If the product is interactive and needs navigation planning, recommend a flowchart. Always explain the purpose, name specific components, and link your answer to the scenario.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Asset logs record every resource used in a media product, tracking file names, formats, sources and copyright permissions.
  • Flowcharts plan the navigation and structure of interactive media products using standard symbols (ovals, rectangles, diamonds, arrows).
  • Both documents ensure organisation and clarity in pre-production — asset logs prevent copyright issues, flowcharts ensure logical user journeys.

Lower band (1-3): A basic response that identifies flowcharts use shapes and arrows with limited discussion of effectiveness or improvements.

lessons.title: Scripts and Storyboards
lessons.description: Script formatting, storyboard layout, shot descriptions, dialogue and stage directions.
lessons.content_html:
Scripts in Media Pre-Production

A script is one of the most important pre-production documents for any media product that involves spoken words, acting, or narration. Scripts are used for films, TV programmes, radio shows, animations, podcasts, and even some advertisements.

The purpose of a script is to provide the cast and crew with all the information they need to perform and film each scene. It tells actors what to say, how to move, and what emotions to convey. It also tells the director and camera operators how scenes should look.

Key Fact

A script contains dialogue (what characters say), stage directions (how characters move and behave), camera directions (shot types and angles), and scene descriptions (setting, time of day, location). Together, these ensure the entire team understands the creative vision.

Professional scripts follow strict formatting conventions:

  • Scene heading (slug line) — written in capitals, stating whether the scene is interior (INT.) or exterior (EXT.), the location, and the time of day. Example: INT. SCHOOL LIBRARY — DAY
  • Action/description — written in present tense, describing what the audience sees and what characters are doing
  • Character name — centred and in capitals above the character’s dialogue
  • Dialogue — centred beneath the character name, showing what they say
  • Parenthetical — brief parenthetical directions in brackets indicating how a line should be delivered (e.g. “angrily”, “whispering”)
  • Transitions — instructions for how one scene moves to the next, e.g. CUT TO:, FADE OUT, DISSOLVE TO:

Scripts can be written using word processing software or specialist screenwriting tools such as Celtx or Final Draft. These dedicated tools automatically format the script to industry standard layout.

Scripts are used by directors, actors, camera operators, sound technicians, and editors. Each person reads the same script but focuses on the information relevant to their role.

Storyboards

A storyboard is a visual plan that looks like a comic strip. It shows the key moments of a media product as a sequence of drawn panels, each representing a different shot or scene.

Key Fact

The purpose of a storyboard is to visually plan the sequence of shots in a moving-image product. It shows the production team what each shot should look like, what camera angles and movements to use, and how scenes flow from one to the next.

Each panel of a storyboard typically includes:

  • Image/sketch — a drawing showing what the camera will see in that shot
  • Shot type — close-up, medium shot, long shot, etc.
  • Camera angle — high angle, low angle, eye level, bird’s eye
  • Camera movement — pan, tilt, zoom, tracking shot, crane shot
  • Dialogue/sound — any dialogue or sound effects that accompany the shot
  • Duration — how long the shot lasts (in seconds)
  • Transitions — how the shot connects to the next (cut, fade, dissolve)
  • Notes — additional instructions for lighting, props, or special effects

Storyboards can be hand drawn on pre-printed templates or created digitally using software such as Storyboarder, Canva, or Boords. Hand drawn storyboards are quick to produce but can be harder to share. Digital versions are easier to edit and distribute.

When to Use Scripts and Storyboards

Scripts are appropriate whenever a media product involves spoken dialogue, narration, or performed actions. A TV drama, podcast, radio advertisement, or animation would all require a script.

Storyboards are appropriate whenever a product involves moving images. Films, TV adverts, animations, music videos, and even some website animations benefit from storyboarding. A printed magazine or a podcast, however, would not need a storyboard.

An effective script uses industry standard formatting, provides clear stage and camera directions, and includes all necessary scene descriptions. It can be improved by adding more detailed parentheticals for actors, including timing notes, or adding a shooting schedule reference for each scene.

An effective storyboard has clear drawings (they do not need to be artistic masterpieces), accurate shot descriptions, and enough panels to cover the full sequence. It can be improved by adding colour to distinguish different locations, including timecodes, or annotating camera movements with arrows.

How Scripts and Storyboards Work Together

In most professional productions, scripts and storyboards are used together. The script provides the dialogue and scene descriptions in written form, while the storyboard translates these into a visual sequence. The director uses both to brief the cast and crew — actors read the script for their lines, camera operators study the storyboard for shot composition.
lessons.exam_tip_html: If the exam gives you a scenario involving a moving-image product, think about whether a script, a storyboard, or both are needed. A film needs both. A podcast needs only a script. A photo shoot might need neither. Always name specific components in your answer — saying “it includes shot types and camera angles” is stronger than just saying “it shows the shots.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Scripts contain dialogue, stage directions, camera directions and scene descriptions. They follow strict formatting conventions including slug lines, character names in capitals, and transitions.
  • Storyboards are visual sequences showing shots, camera angles, movement, dialogue, duration and transitions — like a comic strip of the planned product.
  • Scripts are for any product with spoken words; storyboards are for any product with moving images. Professional productions typically use both together.

lessons.title: Visualisation Diagrams and Wireframes
lessons.description: Planning print and digital layouts with visualisation diagrams and wireframe conventions.
lessons.content_html:
Visualisation Diagrams

A visualisation diagram is a sketch that shows what a static media product will look like. It is used for products that do not involve moving images — for example, a magazine page, a poster, a CD cover, a leaflet, a game interface, or a print advertisement.

The purpose of a visualisation diagram is to show the client and design team the planned layout of the product before it is created. It allows the designer to experiment with positioning text, images and graphic elements, and to get feedback before committing to the final design.

Key Fact

Visualisation diagrams are used for static products (print layouts, posters, DVD covers, game interfaces). They show design ideas and possible layouts with annotations explaining choices such as colour, font and image placement.

A good visualisation diagram includes:

  • Layout sketch — a drawing showing where each element (images, text, logos) will be positioned
  • Annotations — labels and notes explaining design decisions, such as why a particular font or colour has been chosen
  • Colour indications — colour swatches or written descriptions of the intended colour scheme
  • Font/typography choices — the style, size and weight of text to be used
  • Image placeholders — boxes or rough sketches showing where photographs or graphics will go
  • Dimensions — the overall size and proportions of the product

Visualisation diagrams can be created by hand (using pencil, paper and coloured pens) or digitally (using software such as Adobe Illustrator, Photoshop, or Canva). Hand-drawn versions are quick to produce and easy to sketch during meetings, while digital versions look more professional and are easier to edit.

They are used by graphic designers, art directors, marketing teams, and clients. The diagram allows stakeholders to agree on the layout and style before the final product is built, saving time and cost.

Wireframe Layouts

A wireframe is a simplified, skeleton layout of a digital product — most commonly a website or mobile app. It focuses on the structure and positioning of elements rather than the visual design.

Key Fact

The purpose of a wireframe is to plan the structure and layout of a web page or app screen — showing where the navigation, headers, content areas, images and buttons will go — before any visual design (colours, fonts, images) is applied.

Wireframes follow specific conventions:

  • Boxes and rectangles — represent content areas, image placeholders, and buttons
  • Lines of text (or “lorem ipsum”) — indicate where text content will appear, without using real wording
  • Crossed boxes — an “X” through a rectangle indicates an image placeholder
  • Navigation elements — menus, buttons and links are shown in their planned positions
  • No colour or styling — wireframes are deliberately plain (usually black, white and grey) to focus attention on layout, not aesthetics
  • Labels — text labels identify each section (e.g. “Header”, “Main content”, “Sidebar”, “Footer”)

Wireframes can be sketched by hand on paper or created using dedicated tools such as Figma, Balsamiq, or Adobe XD. They are used by web developers, UX designers, project managers, and clients.

Visualisation Diagram vs Wireframe

These two documents are easy to confuse, but they serve different purposes:

  • A visualisation diagram is for static/print products (posters, magazine covers, DVD cases). It includes colour, font choices, and design detail.
  • A wireframe is for digital/interactive products (websites, apps). It is deliberately stripped of visual design to focus on structure and user experience.

An effective visualisation diagram clearly shows the layout with detailed annotations explaining every design choice. It includes colour swatches and font samples so the client can visualise the final product. It can be improved by adding multiple versions showing alternative layouts, including size/dimension annotations, or using digital tools for a cleaner presentation.

An effective wireframe clearly shows the position and size of all page elements, uses consistent conventions (crossed boxes for images, lorem ipsum for text), and is labelled so non-technical stakeholders can understand it. It can be improved by creating wireframes for multiple screen sizes (desktop, tablet, mobile), adding interactive prototyping links between pages, or annotating the user journey.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common exam mistake is mixing up visualisation diagrams and wireframes. Remember: visualisation diagrams = static/print (with colour and design detail), wireframes = digital/interactive (plain layout only). If the scenario is about a website or app, choose a wireframe. If it is about a poster, magazine cover, or DVD case, choose a visualisation diagram.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Visualisation diagrams show the planned layout and design of static products (posters, magazine covers, DVD cases) with colour, font and image annotations.
  • Wireframes show the skeletal structure of digital products (websites, apps) without colour or styling, focusing purely on element placement and user navigation.
  • Both are created in pre-production to get client and team agreement on layout before the final product is built.

lessons.title: Camera Shots, Angles and Movement
lessons.description: Technical filming vocabulary: shot types, camera angles and camera movement for pre-production.
lessons.content_html:
Camera Techniques in Pre-Production

When planning a moving-image media product, the production team must decide which camera shots, angles and movements will be used. These technical decisions are recorded on storyboards and scripts during pre-production and then executed by the camera operator during filming.

Understanding camera terminology is essential for R093. You need to know the different shot types, what they communicate to the audience, and when each would be appropriate in a given scenario.

Shot Types

Shot types describe how much of the subject and setting the camera captures. Moving from widest to closest:

Key Fact

The exam may show you an image and ask you to identify the shot type, or give you a scenario and ask which shot type would be most effective. Learn all shot types and why each is used, not just their names.

  • Extreme Long Shot (ELS) — shows a vast area of landscape or setting. Used to establish location and make subjects appear small and insignificant.
  • Long Shot (LS) — shows the full body of a character within their surroundings. Used to show the character in context.
  • Medium Long Shot (MLS) — frames the character from roughly the knees up. Shows body language while giving some environmental context.
  • Medium Shot (MS) — frames the character from the waist up. The standard “conversational” shot used in interviews and dialogue scenes.
  • Bust Shot — frames the character from the chest/shoulders up. Common in news broadcasts and formal interviews.
  • Close-Up (CU) — fills the frame with the subject’s face (or a single object). Used to show emotion, detail, or importance.
  • Extreme Close-Up (ECU) — shows a very small detail — just the eyes, a hand, or a specific object. Creates intensity and draws attention to a key detail.
  • Two Shot — frames two characters together, often used in dialogue or relationship scenes.
  • Over-the-Shoulder Shot (OTS) — films over one character’s shoulder to show the other character’s face. Creates a sense of conversation and connection.
  • Point of View (POV) — shows what a character sees from their perspective. Makes the audience feel as if they are experiencing events through that character’s eyes.

Camera Angles

Camera angles describe the vertical position of the camera relative to the subject. The angle changes how the audience perceives a character or object.

  • Eye Level — the camera is at the same height as the subject. Creates a neutral, natural feeling — the audience views the subject as an equal.
  • High Angle — the camera looks down on the subject. Makes the subject appear small, weak, vulnerable or inferior.
  • Low Angle — the camera looks up at the subject. Makes the subject appear powerful, dominant, imposing or heroic.
  • Bird’s Eye / Aerial — the camera is positioned directly above, looking straight down. Used for establishing shots or to show the scale of a scene.
  • Worm’s Eye — the camera is positioned at ground level, looking up. Creates an extreme sense of height and power.
  • Dutch Angle / Canted Angle — the camera is tilted to one side, making the horizon appear diagonal. Creates a sense of unease, tension, or disorientation.
Key Fact

Camera angles convey power dynamics. A low angle makes someone look powerful; a high angle makes them look vulnerable. A Dutch angle suggests something is wrong or unsettling. Always link the angle to its effect on the audience in your exam answers.

Camera Movements

Camera movements describe how the camera physically moves during a shot. Movement adds dynamism and can guide the audience’s attention.

  • Pan — the camera rotates horizontally (left to right or right to left) on a fixed point, like turning your head. Used to follow action or reveal a wide scene.
  • Tilt — the camera rotates vertically (up or down) on a fixed point, like nodding your head. Used to reveal height — e.g. tilting up a tall building.
  • Zoom — the camera lens changes focal length to make the subject appear closer (zoom in) or further away (zoom out). The camera itself does not move.
  • Tracking / Dolly Shot — the entire camera moves alongside, towards, or away from the subject, usually on rails or a wheeled dolly. Creates smooth, cinematic movement.
  • Crane Shot — the camera is mounted on a crane and moves vertically through space — rising above or descending into a scene. Used for dramatic reveals.
  • Handheld — the camera is held by the operator without stabilisation, creating a shaky, raw, documentary-style feel. Conveys urgency, chaos, or realism.
  • Steadicam — the camera is mounted on a stabilised harness, allowing smooth movement while the operator walks. Combines the freedom of handheld with the smoothness of tracking.

In the exam, you must explain why a particular camera technique would be used, not just name it. Link the technique to its effect on the audience:

  • A close-up of a character’s face shows their emotion, creating empathy
  • A low angle on a villain makes them appear threatening and powerful
  • A handheld shot in a chase scene increases tension and realism
  • A crane shot rising above a city establishes the setting and creates a sense of scale
  • A Dutch angle during a horror scene creates a feeling of unease and disorientation
lessons.exam_tip_html: When the exam asks about camera techniques, always provide three things: name the technique, describe what it looks like, and explain its effect on the audience. For example: “A low angle shot is where the camera looks up at the subject. This makes the character appear powerful and dominant, which would be effective for introducing the villain.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Shot types control how much of the subject and setting is visible, from extreme long shots (landscape) to extreme close-ups (detail).
  • Camera angles affect how the audience perceives power and status — low angles suggest dominance, high angles suggest vulnerability.
  • Camera movements (pan, tilt, zoom, tracking, crane, handheld) add dynamism and guide audience attention. Always link technique to audience effect in exam answers.

lessons.title: Legal Issues: Copyright, Trademarks and Privacy
lessons.description: Intellectual property, copyright, Creative Commons, privacy laws, defamation and data protection.
lessons.content_html:
Legal Issues in Media Production

Media producers must understand and follow the law when creating, using and publishing content. The R093 specification covers two areas of legal issues: protecting individuals (privacy, defamation, data protection) and intellectual property rights (copyright, trademarks, patents). You do not need to know specific Acts of legislation — the exam tests your understanding of the principles and their impact on media production.

Protecting Individuals

Privacy and Permissions

Media producers must consider people’s right to privacy when recording images or taking photographs:

  • Public places — you generally have the right to film or photograph in public spaces, but you must not harass individuals or invade their privacy
  • Private property — you must obtain permission from the property owner before filming or photographing on private land
  • Publishing images — if you photograph someone and plan to use their image commercially (in an advert, for example), you need their consent — particularly for identifiable individuals
Key Fact

Filming in public is generally allowed, but filming on private property requires the owner’s permission, and using someone’s image for commercial purposes requires their consent. Harassment and invasion of privacy are always illegal.

Defamation

Defamation is making a false statement about someone that damages their reputation. It comes in two forms:

  • Libel — defamation in a written or published form (including websites, social media, newspapers and broadcasts)
  • Slander — defamation in a spoken form (including interviews, podcasts and live broadcasts)

Media producers must ensure that the content they publish is accurate. Publishing false information that harms someone’s reputation can lead to expensive legal action.

Data Protection

Data protection laws give individuals rights over their personal data. Media producers who collect personal information (e.g. names, email addresses, photographs, location data) must:

  • Only collect data for a specific, lawful purpose
  • Keep data accurate and up to date
  • Store data securely
  • Not keep data for longer than necessary
  • Allow individuals to access, correct and delete their data

If a media producer publishes inaccurate personal information or violates someone’s privacy:

  • Impact on the individual — damaged reputation, emotional distress, loss of privacy, potential harassment from the public
  • Impact on the producer — legal action (lawsuits, fines), loss of professional reputation, financial costs of compensation, potential criminal prosecution

Intellectual Property Rights

Intellectual property (IP) refers to creations of the mind that are protected by law. There are three main types relevant to media:

Key Fact

Copyright protects creative works (text, music, images, video, software). Trademarks protect brand identifiers (logos, names, slogans). Patents protect inventions and technical innovations (machines, tools, medicines). Media producers must respect all three.

Copyright (©) — automatically protects original creative works from the moment they are created. The creator has exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute and adapt their work. You cannot use someone else’s copyrighted image, music or text without permission.

Trademarks (™ / ®) — protect product names, logos and business names. You cannot use another company’s trademark in your media product without permission, as this could confuse consumers or damage the brand.

Patents — protect inventions, products and technical processes (e.g. machine tools, medicines, new technologies). Less directly relevant to everyday media production, but important in digital media where software features may be patented.

Using Copyrighted Materials Legally

Media producers who want to use someone else’s work have several legal options:

  • Creative Commons licences — the creator has chosen to share their work under specific conditions (e.g. with attribution, non-commercial use only)
  • Fair dealing — limited use of copyrighted material is allowed for purposes such as criticism, review, news reporting, or education
  • Permissions, fees and licences — the producer contacts the copyright holder and obtains a licence, often paying a fee
  • Watermarks and symbols — copyright holders may use watermarks or the © symbol to indicate their work is protected

If a media producer uses copyrighted material without permission, the consequences can include:

  • Legal action from the copyright holder (lawsuit for damages)
  • The product may have to be removed from distribution or destroyed
  • Financial penalties and compensation payments
  • Damage to the producer’s professional reputation
  • Criminal prosecution in serious cases of piracy or counterfeiting
lessons.exam_tip_html: Legal issue questions often give you a scenario and ask you to identify the legal considerations. Read the scenario carefully — if it mentions using images from the internet, think copyright. If it mentions filming people, think privacy and permissions. If it mentions storing customer data, think data protection. Always explain the impact on both the individual and the media producer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Privacy law requires permission for filming on private property and for commercial use of individuals’ images. Defamation (libel and slander) occurs when false statements damage someone’s reputation.
  • Data protection gives individuals rights over how their personal data is collected, stored and used.
  • Intellectual property is protected by copyright (creative works), trademarks (brand identifiers) and patents (inventions). Copyrighted material can be used legally through Creative Commons licences, fair dealing, or by obtaining paid permission.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of intellectual property protection.
practice_questions.marks:

Award up to 2 marks:
• Libel is defamation in written/published form (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a Creative Commons licence.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• A Creative Commons licence allows creators to share their work with specific permissions/conditions (1)
• It may allow reuse with attribution/credit to the original creator (1)
• Some licences restrict commercial use or modifications (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain why a media producer must consider data protection when creating a marketing campaign that collects customer email addresses.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Email addresses are personal data protected by data protection law (1)
• The producer must only collect data for a specific, stated purpose (1)
• Data must be stored securely and not shared without consent (1)
• Individuals must be able to access, correct or delete their data (1)
• Failure to comply could lead to fines, legal action and reputational damage (1)

practice_questions.text: A student is creating a promotional video for a school event. They want to use a popular song as background music and include photographs of students. Explain the legal issues they would need to consider.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• The popular song is protected by copyright — they cannot use it without permission from the copyright holder (1)
• They could use royalty-free music or music under a Creative Commons licence instead (1)
• They could seek permission/pay a licence fee to use the song (1)
• Photographs of students involve privacy — they need consent/permission from the individuals (or parents for under-18s) (1)
• If the video is published online, data protection applies to identifiable individuals (1)
• They must not publish anything defamatory about any students (1)

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact on both individuals and media producers when copyrighted material is used without permission. Consider legal, financial and reputational consequences in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): A thorough discussion covering multiple consequences for both parties. Legal impacts (lawsuits, prosecution), financial impacts (fines, compensation, lost revenue for the creator), and reputational impacts (damage to professional standing, loss of trust) all discussed with specific examples. Well-structured with clear distinction between impact on individual and producer.
Mid band (4-6): A reasonable discussion identifying several consequences but may focus mainly on one party or one type of impact. Some specific examples.
Lower band (1-3): A basic response identifying that copyright infringement is illegal with limited detail about specific consequences.

lessons.title: Regulation, Certification, Health and Safety
lessons.description: BBFC, ASA, PEGI and Ofcom roles, risk assessments, location recces and production safety.
lessons.content_html:
Regulation, Certification and Classification

The media industry is regulated by several organisations that set standards for content, protect audiences, and ensure media products are appropriate for their intended viewers. The R093 specification requires you to know the roles and responsibilities of four key regulatory bodies, the purpose of regulation, and how it impacts media production.

Regulatory Bodies

Key Fact

There are four regulatory bodies you must know: ASA (advertising), Ofcom (broadcasting and communications), BBFC (films) and PEGI (video games). Each one covers a different type of media product.

The ASA (Advertising Standards Authority) regulates advertising in all forms of media — including TV, radio, print, online, social media and billboards.

  • Ensures adverts are legal, decent, honest and truthful
  • Investigates complaints from the public about misleading or offensive adverts
  • Can require adverts to be changed or withdrawn
  • Works with the Committee of Advertising Practice (CAP) to set advertising codes

Impact on media production: Advertising producers must check that all claims are truthful and evidenced, content is not offensive to the target audience, and any disclaimers are clearly visible. A banned advert wastes budget and damages the brand’s reputation.

Ofcom (The Office of Communications) regulates broadcasting and communication services in the UK — including TV, radio, telecoms and the postal service.

  • Sets standards for what can be broadcast on TV and radio (the Broadcasting Code)
  • Investigates complaints from viewers and listeners
  • Ensures broadcasters do not breach content rules (e.g. showing violent or sexual content before the 9pm watershed)
  • Promotes fair competition in communication markets

Impact on media production: TV and radio producers must comply with Ofcom’s Broadcasting Code. Content shown before the watershed must be suitable for children. Producers must be aware of scheduling restrictions and content guidelines.

The BBFC (British Board of Film Classification) classifies films, cinema trailers, and some online content.

  • U — suitable for all audiences
  • PG — general viewing, but some scenes may be unsuitable for young children
  • 12A / 12 — suitable for 12 years and over (12A allows younger children with an adult in cinemas)
  • 15 — suitable only for 15 years and over
  • 18 — adults only

Impact on media production: Film producers must consider their target audience when creating content. If a film aimed at teenagers receives an 18 certificate, it will lose much of its audience. Producers may edit content to achieve a lower rating.

PEGI (Pan European Game Information) is the rating system for video games across Europe.

  • Uses age ratings: 3, 7, 12, 16, 18
  • Uses content descriptors (icons) showing the type of content: violence, bad language, fear, drugs, sex, discrimination, gambling, in-game purchases
  • Helps consumers (especially parents) make informed choices when buying games

Impact on media production: Game developers must consider the content of their game and the target audience. Including violent or mature content will result in a higher age rating, which may limit the potential market.

Health and Safety in Media Production

Health and safety must be considered in all phases of media production — pre-production, production and post-production. The specification requires you to know common risks and hazards, how to mitigate them, what risk assessments are, and the purpose of location recces.

Key Fact

A risk assessment is a document that identifies potential hazards in a media production, assesses how likely each hazard is to cause harm, and records the actions taken to reduce or eliminate the risk. It must be completed before production begins.

Common Risks and Hazards

  • Electrical hazards — cables, lighting rigs, and equipment must be PAT tested and cables taped down to prevent tripping
  • Manual handling — heavy equipment (cameras, lights, set pieces) must be lifted correctly to avoid injury
  • Working at height — using scaffolding, ladders, or crane equipment requires safety precautions
  • Lone working — crew members working alone in remote locations face additional safety risks
  • Environmental hazards — weather conditions, uneven ground, water, traffic near filming locations
  • Fire risks — hot lights, pyrotechnics, or overcrowded studio spaces

A risk assessment typically includes:

  • A list of identified hazards
  • Who might be harmed and how
  • The level of risk (likelihood and severity)
  • Control measures — actions to reduce or eliminate the risk
  • The person responsible for implementing each control measure

A location recce is a pre-production visit to a potential filming location. The purpose is to:

  • Assess the location’s suitability for the planned shots
  • Identify potential hazards (traffic, water, uneven ground)
  • Check lighting conditions (natural light, power supply for artificial lights)
  • Assess noise levels (nearby roads, airports, construction)
  • Confirm access, parking, and facilities for the crew
  • Take photographs for reference during production planning

Mitigating Health and Safety Risks

Actions media producers take to reduce risk include:

  • Completing a risk assessment before every shoot
  • Conducting a location recce to identify site-specific hazards
  • Ensuring all electrical equipment is PAT tested
  • Providing first aid kits and trained first aiders on set
  • Taping down cables and using cable covers
  • Briefing the crew on safety procedures at the start of each day
  • Ensuring fire extinguishers are available and exit routes are clear
  • Having a buddy system for lone workers
lessons.exam_tip_html: Regulation and health and safety questions often appear in Section B of R093, linked to a specific scenario. When answering, always name the correct regulatory body for the product type in the scenario. For health and safety, identify specific hazards from the scenario and suggest specific control measures — generic answers like “be safe” will not earn marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Four regulatory bodies: ASA (adverts), Ofcom (TV/radio), BBFC (films) and PEGI (games). Each ensures media products meet content standards and are suitable for their audiences.
  • Risk assessments identify hazards and control measures before production. Location recces assess filming locations for suitability and safety.
  • Common hazards include electrical risks, manual handling, working at height, lone working and environmental dangers. All must be mitigated with specific actions.

practice_questions.text: State two purposes of carrying out a location recce.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid purpose (max 2):
• To assess the location’s suitability for filming (1)
• To identify potential hazards (1)
• To check lighting/noise conditions (1)
• To confirm access, parking and facilities (1)
• To take reference photographs (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the BBFC in the media industry.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• The BBFC classifies films and cinema trailers (1)
• It uses age ratings: U, PG, 12A, 12, 15, 18 (1)
• The ratings indicate suitability for different age groups (1)
• It helps protect audiences from unsuitable content (1)
• Films cannot be shown in cinemas without a BBFC classification (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain why a media producer should carry out a risk assessment before filming on location.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• A risk assessment identifies potential hazards at the location (1)
• It assesses the likelihood and severity of each risk (1)
• It records control measures to reduce/eliminate risks (1)
• It protects the safety of cast, crew and the public (1)
• It is a legal requirement / shows the producer has taken reasonable precautions (1)

practice_questions.text: A company is creating a TV advertisement for a new children’s toy. Explain which regulatory bodies would be relevant and describe how regulation would affect the production of this advertisement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• ASA regulates advertising — the advert must be legal, decent, honest and truthful (1)
• The ASA would investigate if the advert makes misleading claims about the toy (1)
• Ofcom regulates TV broadcasting — the advert must comply with scheduling rules (1)
• If shown on TV, it must be appropriate for the time slot (before/after the watershed) (1)
• The content must be suitable for children as the target audience (1)
• The producer must check that no content is harmful, offensive or misleading to young viewers (1)
• Non-compliance could result in the advert being withdrawn, fines, or reputational damage (1)

practice_questions.text: Discuss the importance of health and safety procedures in media production. Consider both pre-production planning (risk assessments, location recces) and on-set practices. Use specific examples of hazards and control measures in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): A thorough discussion covering both pre-production planning and on-set practices. Specific hazards identified (electrical, manual handling, weather, lone working) with matching control measures (PAT testing, cable covers, first aid, buddy systems). Explains the purpose of risk assessments and location recces in detail. Well-structured with reasoned conclusions about why H&S is essential.
Mid band (4-6): A reasonable discussion identifying several hazards and control measures. May focus more on one phase (pre-production or on-set) than the other. Some specific examples.
Lower band (1-3): A basic response that states health and safety is important with few specific examples of hazards or control measures.
